title: What is `min.insync.replicas`, and why does it matter alongside `acks=all`?
shortTitle: What is `min.insync.replicas` and why it matters alongside `acks=all`

s1_definition.profdef: `min.insync.replicas` is a broker and topic configuration that sets the minimum number of in-sync replicas that must acknowledge a write before the write is considered successful when the producer uses `acks=all`. With `acks=all` the producer waits for all current in-sync replicas to persist the record, but it is `min.insync.replicas` that defines how many in-sync replicas must exist for a write to be allowed at all. If the number of in-sync replicas falls below this minimum, the broker rejects writes with a NotEnoughReplicas error, so the two settings together trade availability for durability by refusing to accept data that could not be safely replicated.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India requires that every important ledger entry be signed by at least two independent officers before it counts as recorded. Setting acks all is like Rajesh saying "I will only consider my transfer done once all the on-duty officers have signed." Setting min.insync.replicas to two is the bank's rule that at least two officers must be on duty and signing, otherwise the transaction is refused rather than recorded by a single officer who might then go home with the only copy. Together they guarantee that no transfer is ever acknowledged unless it is safely written in at least two places.
s1_definition.oneliner: min.insync.replicas sets the minimum replicas that must persist a record for an acks=all write to succeed, so together they guarantee durability by refusing writes that cannot be safely replicated.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `min.insync.replicas` is a broker and topic configuration that sets the minimum number of in-sync replicas that must acknowledge a write before the write is considered successful when the producer uses `acks=all`. With `acks=all` the producer waits for all current in-sync replicas to persist the record, but it is `min.insync.replicas` that defines how many in-sync replicas must exist for a write to be allowed at all. If the number of in-sync replicas falls below this minimum, the broker rejects writes with a NotEnoughReplicas error, so the two settings together trade availability for durability by refusing to accept data that could not be safely replicated.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India requires that every important ledger entry be signed by at least two independent officers before it counts as recorded. Setting acks all is like Rajesh saying "I will only consider my transfer done once all the on-duty officers have signed." Setting min.insync.replicas to two is the bank's rule that at least two officers must be on duty and signing, otherwise the transaction is refused rather than recorded by a single officer who might then go home with the only copy. Together they guarantee that no transfer is ever acknowledged unless it is safely written in at least two places.

**One line to remember:** min.insync.replicas sets the minimum replicas that must persist a record for an acks=all write to succeed, so together they guarantee durability by refusing writes that cannot be safely replicated.

sections.s2_technical:
Begin with the in-sync replica set, the ISR. Each partition has one leader and several follower replicas. The ISR is the set of replicas that are fully caught up with the leader. When a follower falls too far behind, it is removed from the ISR, and when it catches up, it rejoins. The ISR is therefore the set of replicas currently safe to acknowledge a write.

Now the producer's acks setting. With acks equal to zero the producer does not wait at all, with acks equal to one it waits only for the leader, and with acks equal to all it waits for every replica in the ISR to persist the record before the broker acknowledges. Acks all gives the strongest durability because the record is on every currently in-sync replica. But acks all alone has a subtle gap: if the ISR has shrunk to just the leader, then acks all means acks on one replica, and if that leader then fails, the record is lost even though the producer thought it was safe.

This is exactly where min.insync.replicas comes in. It tells the broker the minimum size the ISR must have for an acks all write to be accepted. If the ISR drops below this number, the broker rejects the write with NotEnoughReplicas rather than acknowledging a write that is not sufficiently replicated. So acks all answers "wait for all in-sync replicas," and min.insync.replicas answers "but there must be at least this many in-sync replicas, or do not accept the write at all." The two settings only deliver strong durability when used together.

The standard safe configuration for a bank is replication factor three, min.insync.replicas two, and acks all. With these, a write must be on at least two replicas to be acknowledged, so the cluster can lose one broker and still have the data and still accept writes. If it loses two brokers, the ISR drops to one, below the minimum of two, so the partition stops accepting writes, which is the deliberate choice to refuse data rather than risk losing it. This is the classic durability-versus-availability trade-off: a higher minimum is safer but makes writes unavailable sooner when brokers fail.

In code you set these at different layers. The producer sets `acks=all`. The topic or broker sets `min.insync.replicas`, for example as a topic config `min.insync.replicas=2`. The senior nuances are that min.insync.replicas without acks all is nearly useless, because acks one never checks the ISR size, so the two must be paired; that replication factor must be strictly greater than min.insync.replicas to tolerate a broker loss while still accepting writes; and that setting min.insync.replicas equal to the replication factor maximizes durability but means losing even one broker halts writes, which is usually too fragile.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India ran its transfers topic with acks all but min.insync.replicas of one. During an incident two brokers were lost, the ISR shrank to just the leader, acks all effectively meant acks on one replica, and when that leader also failed, acknowledged transfers were lost. This is exactly the gap that acks all alone leaves and that min.insync.replicas closes.

Problem 2 — The team moved to replication factor three, min.insync.replicas two, and acks all. Now a write must be on at least two replicas to be acknowledged, so a single broker loss is tolerated with no data loss and writes continue, and a two-broker loss deliberately halts writes rather than risking loss. This is exactly how the two settings together deliver durability.

We simulate this in plain Java. A `PartitionReplicas` tracks the ISR and a leader; a `WriteBroker` accepts a write only if acks all is satisfied by every ISR member and the ISR size meets min.insync.replicas, otherwise it rejects with a NotEnoughReplicas error. The demo writes with a healthy ISR, then shrinks the ISR below the minimum to show the rejection. The code will show: a `PartitionReplicas`, a `NotEnoughReplicasException`, the `WriteBroker`, and a demo.

# application.yml — producer acks=all; topic min.insync.replicas=2 (set separately)
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      acks: all                     # wait for ALL in-sync replicas
      retries: 2147483647
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a partition with replication factor three on brokers one, two, and three, min.insync.replicas of two, acks all, and three write attempts as brokers fail.

Step 1: Initially all three brokers are in the ISR, so the ISR size is three. The first transfer write arrives with acks all. The broker checks that the ISR size three is at least the minimum two, persists to all three in-sync replicas, and acknowledges. The write is safely on three replicas.

Step 2: Broker three fails and drops out of the ISR, leaving brokers one and two, so the ISR size is two. The second transfer write arrives. The broker checks that two is still at least the minimum two, persists to both remaining in-sync replicas, and acknowledges. A single broker loss is tolerated with no data loss.

Step 3: Broker two also fails and drops out of the ISR, leaving only broker one, so the ISR size is one.

Step 4: The third transfer write arrives with acks all. The broker checks the ISR size, finds one, which is below the minimum of two, and refuses the write, throwing NotEnoughReplicas instead of acknowledging a record that would sit on only a single replica.

Step 5: The producer sees the rejection and does not get a false acknowledgement. The bank has deliberately chosen durability over availability: rather than record a transfer on one fragile replica that could be lost if that broker also fails, the partition stops accepting writes until a replica rejoins the ISR.

```
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Write OK 'TRANSFER SAV2001->CUR3001 50000' persisted to ISR=[broker-1, broker-2, broker-3] (size 3 >= 2)
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Write OK 'TRANSFER CUR3001->SAV2001 20000' persisted to ISR=[broker-1, broker-2] (size 2 >= 2)
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [SEVERE ] Write rejected: ISR=1 < min.insync.replicas=2 — rejecting write to avoid acknowledging unsafe data: 'TRANSFER SAV2001->CUR3001 99999'
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [WARNING] Durability chosen over availability: refuse rather than risk loss.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer (acks=all) ──write──→ Leader broker
                                   │ check: ISR size >= min.insync.replicas (2)?
     ┌─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┐
     ▼                             ▼                              ▼
  ISR=3 (b1,b2,b3)          ISR=2 (b1,b2)                 ISR=1 (b1 only)
  3 >= 2 ✓                  2 >= 2 ✓                      1 >= 2 ✗
  persist to all 3          persist to both               REJECT
  → ACK                     → ACK (tolerates 1 loss)      NotEnoughReplicas
                                                          (refuse unsafe write)
  acks=all = "wait for all ISR"; min.insync.replicas = "ISR must be at least N"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
min.insync.replicas is the broker and topic setting that defines the minimum number of in-sync replicas that must persist a record for a write to succeed when the producer uses acks all, and the reason it matters is that acks all by itself has a quiet gap. With acks all the producer waits for every replica currently in the in-sync set to persist the record, which sounds fully safe, but if the in-sync set has shrunk to just the leader, then all means one, and if that leader then fails, an acknowledged record is lost even though the producer believed it was durable.

min.insync.replicas closes that gap. It tells the broker the minimum size the in-sync set must have for an acks all write to be accepted. If the in-sync set drops below that number, the broker rejects the write with a NotEnoughReplicas error rather than acknowledging data that is not sufficiently replicated. So I describe the two settings as a pair: acks all says wait for all the in-sync replicas, and min.insync.replicas says but there must be at least this many in-sync replicas, or do not accept the write at all. One without the other is incomplete; in particular min.insync.replicas does nothing under acks one, because acks one never checks the in-sync set size.

The standard safe configuration I use in a bank is replication factor three, min.insync.replicas two, and acks all. With that, a write must be on at least two replicas to be acknowledged, so the cluster can lose one broker and still hold the data and still accept writes. If it loses two brokers, the in-sync set drops to one, below the minimum of two, so the partition deliberately stops accepting writes. That is the heart of the trade-off: it is the conscious choice to refuse data rather than risk losing it. I also keep the rule that replication factor must be strictly greater than min.insync.replicas, because otherwise even a single broker loss halts writes, which is too fragile for most systems.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, we once ran transfers with acks all but min.insync.replicas of one, and during an incident two brokers were lost, the in-sync set shrank to the leader, and when the leader also failed we lost acknowledged transfers, which is a nightmare for a bank. We moved to replication factor three, min.insync.replicas two, and acks all, so now a single broker loss is tolerated with no data loss and writes continue, while a two-broker loss halts writes rather than risking loss. The senior framing I give is that acks all is only as durable as the in-sync set is deep, and min.insync.replicas is what guarantees that depth, so for anything representing money I always set them together with a replication factor that leaves headroom to survive a broker failure.
